description: We are a team of students interested in space, science, technology, and problem-solving. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are working on “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.” Our goal is to create a useful software idea that can help monitor astronauts’ health and support them during space missions.
summary: ASTRA (Astronaut Self-assessment, Tracking and Response Assistant) is an offline-first health-monitoring and medical decision-support system for long-duration missions such as Mars transit or lunar bases. Astronauts record vital signs, symptoms, sleep, mood, exercise and nutrition. ASTRA compares each reading with that astronaut's own approved baseline, explains its findings, raises alerts and guides the crew through preloaded response procedures. It runs as two connected systems from one codebase. The onboard Crew Side works with no contact with Earth, and the Crew Medical Officer monitors the whole crew locally. The Earth Side lets flight surgeons and administrators review records sent by a secure store-and-forward link that loses nothing during communication outages. ASTRA supports decisions; it is not an autonomous doctor.
details:
Project details

What it does and how it works

- Recording: each astronaut uses a browser on the spacecraft network to record vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, SpO₂, temperature, respiration), symptoms, sleep, a private mood and stress check-in, exercise, and food and water. Simulated wearables and medical devices feed the same pipeline.

- One validation path: every input goes through one validation pipeline that checks units, plausible ranges, timestamps and permissions before saving.

- Assessment: an explainable rules engine compares readings with each astronaut's own approved baseline instead of population averages. It produces a status: no concern, reassessment, medical review or urgent. Each status comes with findings, its limitations and links to evidence.

- Response: urgent findings open medical events with preloaded procedures, verification checklists, an escalation path, structured medical reports and a full audit trail.

- Two sides:

- The onboard Crew Side is the authoritative database and keeps working with no Earth contact.

- The Earth Side receives records through a signed, acknowledged synchronization API.

- Records are saved locally first. A database trigger queues each one in the same transaction, and a background service sends them whenever the link exists, with retries and duplicate protection.

- Original measurement times are always preserved, and Earth never edits onboard records. Flight surgeons reply with separate, signed follow-up notes that are delivered to the CMO.

- Outage demo: a CMO-only control simulates losing contact with Earth. The crew keeps working, records queue up, and when the link is restored they arrive

on Earth with their original times.

Benefits

- Crew health care continues during communication blackouts and with signal delays of several minutes each way.

- Personal baselines catch changes that population thresholds ins why it was raised.

- Role-based access protects privacy. Behavioural-health check-ins are visible only to the astronaut and the flight surgeon; the CMO sees only that an

entry exists.

- Ground teams always know how fresh their data is and never mistake delayed data for live data.

- It runs on ordinary hardware with no internet or cloud servi

Intended impact

ASTRA aims to show how missions beyond low Earth orbit could move routine health monitoring and first-line medical response onto the spacecraft. It

supports the crew's autonomy while keeping ground medical expe The same design could serve remote or isolated settings onEarth, such as Antarctic stations, ships and disaster areas.

Tools, languages and technology

- Backend: Python with Starlette, Pydantic and Uvicorn; SQLitel schema; JWT sessions; scrypt password hashing; HMAC-SHA256signing between the two servers.

- Frontend: React and TypeScript built with Vite; a hand-writtht and dark themes; a Progressive Web App service worker foroffline loading.

- Testing: pytest, with 91 backend tests including integrationers.

- Deployment and demo: Cloudflare Tunnel for the public demo; Windows batch and PowerShell launchers.

- Hardware: a standard Windows PC. All devices are simulated tal device formats; no physical hardware was tested.

- Data: an evidence base drawn from NASA human-research sources. All demo data is synthetic.

What makes it creative

- It treats the spacecraft and Earth as two equal systems, eacather than a cloud app with an offline mode.

- It captures changes with database triggers, so no health record can be saved without being queued, and needs no changes to the medical logic.

- Original health observations can't be changed, and later clite signed notes.

- Judges can test a real communication outage with one clearly labelled button, with no unplugged cables or stopped servers.

- Status colours are reserved for medical meaning only, in bot

Factors the team considered

- Safety and honesty: decision support only; synthetic rules are labelled as such and no clinical thresholds were invented.

- Privacy: behavioural-health data, role scoping, and least-prs.

- Data integrity: unique IDs, original timestamps, acknowledgements, duplicate protection and audit logs.

- Security: signed server-to-server requests, encrypted transp machine, and rate limits on the public demo.

- Communication delay and outages.

- Usability for tired crew members: clear status colours, measast, and light and dark themes.

- Running on modest onboard hardware without internet.

- Honesty about limitations: simulated devices, the demo passw account changes made on Earth are not sent to the spacecraft.
